culture
Architectural marvels from Faisal Mosque to neighbourhood gems
Islamabad was designed from the beginning as a capital city that would embody Pakistan's Islamic identity in its very architecture. The city's masterplan, developed by Greek architect Constantinos Doxiadis in the 1960s, allocated prominent sites to mosques in every sector, and the government invested significantly in creating places of worship that would reflect both Islamic heritage and the modern nation's ambitions. The result is a city where mosques are architectural landmarks, not just functional spaces. The spectrum of mosque architecture in Islamabad spans from the world-famous Faisal Mosque — a modernist masterpiece that reimagined what a mosque could look like in the 20th century — to centuries-old neighbourhood masjids that predate the city's founding. Each tells a different story about the Islamic tradition's engagement with architecture, space, and community across different eras and influences. Visiting mosques in Islamabad as a non-Muslim visitor is generally welcomed, though proper etiquette is essential: remove shoes before entering, dress modestly with arms and legs covered, and women should cover their hair. The main prayer times (especially Jumu'ah on Friday) are the most atmospheric times to experience these spaces but require extra care about space and timing. Most major mosques have separate entrances and areas for non-Muslim visitors.
1

## Faisal Mosque
Shah Faisal Avenue, at the foot of Margalla Hills
The Faisal Mosque is Pakistan's most iconic building and one of the most architecturally significant mosques built anywhere in the world in the 20th century. Designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay and completed in 1988, the mosque abandoned the traditional dome in favour of a triangular tent-like prayer hall inspired by Bedouin tents, surrounded by four 90-metre minarets that frame the Margalla Hills behind. The main prayer hall accommodates 10,000 worshippers, with the surrounding courtyard, porticoes, and grounds able to hold an additional 200,000 for major occasions. The white marble and geometric tile work are breathtaking at any time of day.
World's largest mosque (at completion in 1988)Turkish modernist design 90m minarets Bedouin tent form
**Fun Fact:**The Faisal Mosque was funded by a generous donation of $130 million from Saudi King Faisal bin Abdulaziz, after whom it is named — he was assassinated in 1975 before its completion.
2

## Masjid-e-Aqsa
F-17, Top City-1
The Masjid-e-Aqsa in Top City is Islamabad's most recently completed grand mosque and draws inspiration from Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa mosque in both name and architectural spirit. The blue-domed structure and its polished marble courtyard represent contemporary Islamic architecture at its most accomplished in Pakistan's capital region. The landscaped gardens around the mosque — with fountains and geometric planting beds — create a serene approach that builds anticipation before the main entrance. Friday prayers here draw thousands from the surrounding housing society and are among the most well-attended in the broader Islamabad-Rawalpindi region.
Contemporary design Blue dome Landscaped gardens Large capacity
**Fun Fact:**The mosque's construction used marble from Balochistan's Ziarat region — the same source that has supplied Pakistan's finest marble since the Mughal era.
3

## Lal Masjid
Sector G-6, near Aabpara
Lal Masjid (the Red Mosque) is Islamabad's most historically significant — and controversial — place of worship. Built in 1965, it is one of the oldest mosques in the capital and played a central role in Pakistani religious and political life. The mosque complex includes the Jamia Hafsa madrassa for women and the Jamia Fareedia for men. The distinctive red sandstone exterior, from which the mosque takes its name, makes it architecturally distinctive among Islamabad's predominantly white marble mosques. The library within the complex contains rare Islamic manuscripts and texts, and the mosque has been a centre for Islamic scholarship for six decades.
Red sandstone exterior 1965 construction Historical significance Islamic library
**Fun Fact:**Lal Masjid's red colour comes from natural red sandstone quarried in Rawalpindi's Attock district — the material was chosen to distinguish it from the planned white marble mosque (Faisal) that would later dominate the skyline.
4

## Centaurus Mosque
The Centaurus Complex, Jinnah Avenue, Blue Area
The mosque within The Centaurus complex is a remarkable integration of religious space and contemporary urban architecture. Located at the base of Islamabad's tallest building — the 38-floor Centaurus tower — the mosque serves the thousands of workers, shoppers, and residents in the complex daily. The prayer hall uses high-quality marble, carved wooden screens, and calligraphic panels to create an interior of genuine spiritual quality despite its urban-commercial context. The muezzin's call here echoes off the glass facades of surrounding towers in a distinctly 21st-century urban soundscape.
Urban integration Contemporary design Marble interior Blue Area location
**Fun Fact:**The Centaurus Mosque can be seen from all four sides of the tower complex — it was deliberately positioned by the architects at the centre of the development to place Islamic worship at the heart of Islamabad's commercial district.
5

## Al-Huda Mosque
G-10/4, Islamabad
The Al-Huda Mosque in G-10 is the home mosque of the Al-Huda International Welfare Foundation, one of Pakistan's most influential Islamic education organisations. The mosque complex is notable for its educational programmes — particularly the Quran and Islamic studies courses for women that have drawn students from across Pakistan and the diaspora. The architecture is functional and serene, centred around a well-lit prayer hall with a separate, thoughtfully designed women's prayer area. The rose garden in the mosque grounds is maintained with care and is in full bloom from February through April.
Al-Huda Institute Women's education programme Rose garden Quran courses
**Fun Fact:**Al-Huda's founder, Dr. Farhat Hashmi, built the institute's reputation on audio and video recordings of Quran tafseer (interpretation) that spread across Pakistan through cassettes in the 1980s before the internet existed.
6

## Aiwan-e-Sadr (Presidential) Mosque
Diplomatic Enclave, Constitution Avenue
The mosque within the Presidential estate grounds represents state-level Islamic architecture at its finest. Though access is limited to official functions and Jumu'ah prayers, the exterior is visible from Constitution Avenue and forms part of Islamabad's ceremonial landscape alongside the Parliament, Supreme Court, and Ministry buildings. The architecture blends classical Islamic arches and calligraphy with the formal language of state buildings — creating a uniquely official variant of religious architecture found only in purpose-built capitals like Islamabad, Riyadh, and Putrajaya.
Presidential estate State architecture Constitution Avenue Ceremonial landscape
**Fun Fact:**The Presidential Mosque was designed to align visually with the Faisal Mosque's minarets when viewed from Constitution Avenue — creating a deliberate axis of Islamic spiritual authority through the capital's ceremonial core.
7

## Grand Mosque — Diplomatic Enclave
Diplomatic Enclave, near Ambassador Hotels
The Grand Mosque serving Islamabad's Diplomatic Enclave community is notable for its international congregation — on Fridays, worshippers from dozens of countries gather here, making it one of the most culturally diverse mosques in South Asia. The Arabic, Persian, and South Asian architectural elements are blended in a way that reflects the enclave's international character. The calligraphy panels inside the prayer hall are in multiple scripts — Arabic, Urdu, and Persian — a rare typographic feature. The mosque's muezzin is widely considered to have one of the finest recitation voices in Islamabad.
International congregation Multi-script calligraphy Diplomatic community Fine recitation
**Fun Fact:**The Diplomatic Enclave mosque's Friday sermon is delivered in both Arabic and English — one of the very few mosques in Pakistan to offer bilingual khutbah for its international congregation.
8

## Bahria Town Grand Mosque
Bahria Town Phase 8
The grand mosque at the heart of Bahria Town Phase 8 is the architectural centrepiece of Pakistan's largest housing development. Designed to accommodate Bahria Town's enormous resident population, the mosque's white marble dome and twin minarets are visible from across the development and serve as a navigational landmark. The complex includes a large wuzu (ablution) facility, covered porticoes for outdoor prayer in monsoon season, and a madrassa for children. The scale of Friday prayers here — drawing worshippers from Bahria's entire western Islamabad community — creates one of the city region's most impressive religious gatherings.
Bahria Town landmark Large capacity White marble dome Community anchor
**Fun Fact:**Bahria Town's mosque complex was built at a cost reportedly exceeding Rs 200 million — part of the developer's strategy to create a self-sufficient township with institutions of spiritual, educational, and commercial gravity.
9

## Masjid Bilal — I-8 Markaz
I-8 Markaz, Islamabad
Masjid Bilal in I-8 is the neighbourhood mosque that best represents the lived religious life of Islamabad's working and middle-class residential sectors. Without the grand scale of Faisal Mosque or the diplomatic prestige of the Enclave mosque, Masjid Bilal serves its immediate community with warmth and consistency — five daily prayers, Quran classes for children, and a local imam known for his accessible and relevant Friday sermons. The architecture is modest but well-maintained, with a small courtyard garden that elderly residents use for morning walks after Fajr prayer.
Neighbourhood community mosque Accessible sermons Children's classes Daily community life
**Fun Fact:**Masjid Bilal was built by community fundraising in 1975 — each household in the original I-8 sector contributed to its construction, making it literally a collectively owned community institution.
10

## Blue Area Juma Mosque
Blue Area, Jinnah Avenue
The central mosque in Islamabad's commercial Blue Area serves the thousands of office workers, shopkeepers, and visitors who populate Pakistan's most important business district. The mosque fills completely at every Jumu'ah prayer as hundreds pour out of surrounding office towers to attend. The architecture is functional modernism — clean lines, quality marble, and excellent acoustics. The location at the heart of government and corporate Islamabad means Friday sermons here occasionally address national affairs and Islamic guidance on contemporary issues facing Pakistan's professional class.
Business district mosque High weekday attendance Clean modernist design Corporate congregation
**Fun Fact:**The Blue Area mosque experiences its highest attendance during Ramadan Tarawih prayers — the cooler nights during Ramadan in Islamabad make the outdoor overflow area pleasant, and attendance often exceeds 3,000 on peak nights.

## Final Thoughts
Islamabad's mosques form a spiritual geography that is inseparable from the city's identity. The Faisal Mosque stands at the northern end of the capital's ceremonial axis as the most recognisable building in Pakistan, while neighbourhood mosques like Masjid Bilal in I-8 represent the daily texture of Islamic community life across the sectors. Between these poles lies a remarkable range of architectural approaches to the same spiritual purpose. For visitors, the single most rewarding mosque experience is arriving at the Faisal Mosque at dawn for Fajr prayer — the light on the white marble, the echo of the call across the courtyard, and the Margalla Hills emerging from darkness behind the minarets is an experience of extraordinary beauty and spiritual power. Equally moving is attending Friday Jumu'ah at Lal Masjid, where the weight of history and decades of community memory fill every corner of the red sandstone space.
10

culture
Architectural marvels from Faisal Mosque to neighbourhood gems
Islamabad was designed from the beginning as a capital city that would embody Pakistan's Islamic identity in its very architecture. The city's masterplan, developed by Greek architect Constantinos Doxiadis in the 1960s, allocated prominent sites to mosques in every sector, and the government invested significantly in creating places of worship that would reflect both Islamic heritage and the modern nation's ambitions. The result is a city where mosques are architectural landmarks, not just functional spaces. The spectrum of mosque architecture in Islamabad spans from the world-famous Faisal Mosque — a modernist masterpiece that reimagined what a mosque could look like in the 20th century — to centuries-old neighbourhood masjids that predate the city's founding. Each tells a different story about the Islamic tradition's engagement with architecture, space, and community across different eras and influences. Visiting mosques in Islamabad as a non-Muslim visitor is generally welcomed, though proper etiquette is essential: remove shoes before entering, dress modestly with arms and legs covered, and women should cover their hair. The main prayer times (especially Jumu'ah on Friday) are the most atmospheric times to experience these spaces but require extra care about space and timing. Most major mosques have separate entrances and areas for non-Muslim visitors.
1
texts.1:
## Faisal Mosque
Shah Faisal Avenue, at the foot of Margalla Hills
The Faisal Mosque is Pakistan's most iconic building and one of the most architecturally significant mosques built anywhere in the world in the 20th century. Designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay and completed in 1988, the mosque abandoned the traditional dome in favour of a triangular tent-like prayer hall inspired by Bedouin tents, surrounded by four 90-metre minarets that frame the Margalla Hills behind. The main prayer hall accommodates 10,000 worshippers, with the surrounding courtyard, porticoes, and grounds able to hold an additional 200,000 for major occasions. The white marble and geometric tile work are breathtaking at any time of day.
World's largest mosque (at completion in 1988)Turkish modernist design 90m minarets Bedouin tent form
**Fun Fact:**The Faisal Mosque was funded by a generous donation of $130 million from Saudi King Faisal bin Abdulaziz, after whom it is named — he was assassinated in 1975 before its completion.
2
texts.2:
## Masjid-e-Aqsa
F-17, Top City-1
The Masjid-e-Aqsa in Top City is Islamabad's most recently completed grand mosque and draws inspiration from Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa mosque in both name and architectural spirit. The blue-domed structure and its polished marble courtyard represent contemporary Islamic architecture at its most accomplished in Pakistan's capital region. The landscaped gardens around the mosque — with fountains and geometric planting beds — create a serene approach that builds anticipation before the main entrance. Friday prayers here draw thousands from the surrounding housing society and are among the most well-attended in the broader Islamabad-Rawalpindi region.
Contemporary design Blue dome Landscaped gardens Large capacity
**Fun Fact:**The mosque's construction used marble from Balochistan's Ziarat region — the same source that has supplied Pakistan's finest marble since the Mughal era.
3
texts.3:
## Lal Masjid
Sector G-6, near Aabpara
Lal Masjid (the Red Mosque) is Islamabad's most historically significant — and controversial — place of worship. Built in 1965, it is one of the oldest mosques in the capital and played a central role in Pakistani religious and political life. The mosque complex includes the Jamia Hafsa madrassa for women and the Jamia Fareedia for men. The distinctive red sandstone exterior, from which the mosque takes its name, makes it architecturally distinctive among Islamabad's predominantly white marble mosques. The library within the complex contains rare Islamic manuscripts and texts, and the mosque has been a centre for Islamic scholarship for six decades.
Red sandstone exterior 1965 construction Historical significance Islamic library
**Fun Fact:**Lal Masjid's red colour comes from natural red sandstone quarried in Rawalpindi's Attock district — the material was chosen to distinguish it from the planned white marble mosque (Faisal) that would later dominate the skyline.
4
texts.4:
## Centaurus Mosque
The Centaurus Complex, Jinnah Avenue, Blue Area
The mosque within The Centaurus complex is a remarkable integration of religious space and contemporary urban architecture. Located at the base of Islamabad's tallest building — the 38-floor Centaurus tower — the mosque serves the thousands of workers, shoppers, and residents in the complex daily. The prayer hall uses high-quality marble, carved wooden screens, and calligraphic panels to create an interior of genuine spiritual quality despite its urban-commercial context. The muezzin's call here echoes off the glass facades of surrounding towers in a distinctly 21st-century urban soundscape.
Urban integration Contemporary design Marble interior Blue Area location
**Fun Fact:**The Centaurus Mosque can be seen from all four sides of the tower complex — it was deliberately positioned by the architects at the centre of the development to place Islamic worship at the heart of Islamabad's commercial district.
5
texts.5:
## Al-Huda Mosque
G-10/4, Islamabad
The Al-Huda Mosque in G-10 is the home mosque of the Al-Huda International Welfare Foundation, one of Pakistan's most influential Islamic education organisations. The mosque complex is notable for its educational programmes — particularly the Quran and Islamic studies courses for women that have drawn students from across Pakistan and the diaspora. The architecture is functional and serene, centred around a well-lit prayer hall with a separate, thoughtfully designed women's prayer area. The rose garden in the mosque grounds is maintained with care and is in full bloom from February through April.
Al-Huda Institute Women's education programme Rose garden Quran courses
**Fun Fact:**Al-Huda's founder, Dr. Farhat Hashmi, built the institute's reputation on audio and video recordings of Quran tafseer (interpretation) that spread across Pakistan through cassettes in the 1980s before the internet existed.
6
texts.6:
## Aiwan-e-Sadr (Presidential) Mosque
Diplomatic Enclave, Constitution Avenue
The mosque within the Presidential estate grounds represents state-level Islamic architecture at its finest. Though access is limited to official functions and Jumu'ah prayers, the exterior is visible from Constitution Avenue and forms part of Islamabad's ceremonial landscape alongside the Parliament, Supreme Court, and Ministry buildings. The architecture blends classical Islamic arches and calligraphy with the formal language of state buildings — creating a uniquely official variant of religious architecture found only in purpose-built capitals like Islamabad, Riyadh, and Putrajaya.
Presidential estate State architecture Constitution Avenue Ceremonial landscape
**Fun Fact:**The Presidential Mosque was designed to align visually with the Faisal Mosque's minarets when viewed from Constitution Avenue — creating a deliberate axis of Islamic spiritual authority through the capital's ceremonial core.
7
texts.7:
## Grand Mosque — Diplomatic Enclave
Diplomatic Enclave, near Ambassador Hotels
The Grand Mosque serving Islamabad's Diplomatic Enclave community is notable for its international congregation — on Fridays, worshippers from dozens of countries gather here, making it one of the most culturally diverse mosques in South Asia. The Arabic, Persian, and South Asian architectural elements are blended in a way that reflects the enclave's international character. The calligraphy panels inside the prayer hall are in multiple scripts — Arabic, Urdu, and Persian — a rare typographic feature. The mosque's muezzin is widely considered to have one of the finest recitation voices in Islamabad.
International congregation Multi-script calligraphy Diplomatic community Fine recitation
**Fun Fact:**The Diplomatic Enclave mosque's Friday sermon is delivered in both Arabic and English — one of the very few mosques in Pakistan to offer bilingual khutbah for its international congregation.
8
texts.8:
## Bahria Town Grand Mosque
Bahria Town Phase 8
The grand mosque at the heart of Bahria Town Phase 8 is the architectural centrepiece of Pakistan's largest housing development. Designed to accommodate Bahria Town's enormous resident population, the mosque's white marble dome and twin minarets are visible from across the development and serve as a navigational landmark. The complex includes a large wuzu (ablution) facility, covered porticoes for outdoor prayer in monsoon season, and a madrassa for children. The scale of Friday prayers here — drawing worshippers from Bahria's entire western Islamabad community — creates one of the city region's most impressive religious gatherings.
Bahria Town landmark Large capacity White marble dome Community anchor
**Fun Fact:**Bahria Town's mosque complex was built at a cost reportedly exceeding Rs 200 million — part of the developer's strategy to create a self-sufficient township with institutions of spiritual, educational, and commercial gravity.
9
texts.9:
## Masjid Bilal — I-8 Markaz
I-8 Markaz, Islamabad
Masjid Bilal in I-8 is the neighbourhood mosque that best represents the lived religious life of Islamabad's working and middle-class residential sectors. Without the grand scale of Faisal Mosque or the diplomatic prestige of the Enclave mosque, Masjid Bilal serves its immediate community with warmth and consistency — five daily prayers, Quran classes for children, and a local imam known for his accessible and relevant Friday sermons. The architecture is modest but well-maintained, with a small courtyard garden that elderly residents use for morning walks after Fajr prayer.
Neighbourhood community mosque Accessible sermons Children's classes Daily community life
**Fun Fact:**Masjid Bilal was built by community fundraising in 1975 — each household in the original I-8 sector contributed to its construction, making it literally a collectively owned community institution.
10
texts.10:
## Blue Area Juma Mosque
Blue Area, Jinnah Avenue
The central mosque in Islamabad's commercial Blue Area serves the thousands of office workers, shopkeepers, and visitors who populate Pakistan's most important business district. The mosque fills completely at every Jumu'ah prayer as hundreds pour out of surrounding office towers to attend. The architecture is functional modernism — clean lines, quality marble, and excellent acoustics. The location at the heart of government and corporate Islamabad means Friday sermons here occasionally address national affairs and Islamic guidance on contemporary issues facing Pakistan's professional class.
Business district mosque High weekday attendance Clean modernist design Corporate congregation
**Fun Fact:**The Blue Area mosque experiences its highest attendance during Ramadan Tarawih prayers — the cooler nights during Ramadan in Islamabad make the outdoor overflow area pleasant, and attendance often exceeds 3,000 on peak nights.
texts.11:
## Final Thoughts
Islamabad's mosques form a spiritual geography that is inseparable from the city's identity. The Faisal Mosque stands at the northern end of the capital's ceremonial axis as the most recognisable building in Pakistan, while neighbourhood mosques like Masjid Bilal in I-8 represent the daily texture of Islamic community life across the sectors. Between these poles lies a remarkable range of architectural approaches to the same spiritual purpose. For visitors, the single most rewarding mosque experience is arriving at the Faisal Mosque at dawn for Fajr prayer — the light on the white marble, the echo of the call across the courtyard, and the Margalla Hills emerging from darkness behind the minarets is an experience of extraordinary beauty and spiritual power. Equally moving is attending Friday Jumu'ah at Lal Masjid, where the weight of history and decades of community memory fill every corner of the red sandstone space.
10

**Fun Fact:**The Diplomatic Enclave mosque's Friday sermon is delivered in both Arabic and English — one of the very few mosques in Pakistan to offer bilingual khutbah for its international congregation.
8

## Bahria Town Grand Mosque
Bahria Town Phase 8
The grand mosque at the heart of Bahria Town Phase 8 is the architectural centrepiece of Pakistan's largest housing development. Designed to accommodate Bahria Town's enormous resident population, the mosque's white marble dome and twin minarets are visible from across the development and serve as a navigational landmark. The complex includes a large wuzu (ablution) facility, covered porticoes for outdoor prayer in monsoon season, and a madrassa for children. The scale of Friday prayers here — drawing worshippers from Bahria's entire western Islamabad community — creates one of the city region's most impressive religious gatherings.
Bahria Town landmark Large capacity White marble dome Community anchor
**Fun Fact:**Bahria Town's mosque complex was built at a cost reportedly exceeding Rs 200 million — part of the developer's strategy to create a self-sufficient township with institutions of spiritual, educational, and commercial gravity.
9

## Masjid Bilal — I-8 Markaz
I-8 Markaz, Islamabad
Masjid Bilal in I-8 is the neighbourhood mosque that best represents the lived religious life of Islamabad's working and middle-class residential sectors. Without the grand scale of Faisal Mosque or the diplomatic prestige of the Enclave mosque, Masjid Bilal serves its immediate community with warmth and consistency — five daily prayers, Quran classes for children, and a local imam known for his accessible and relevant Friday sermons. The architecture is modest but well-maintained, with a small courtyard garden that elderly residents use for morning walks after Fajr prayer.
Neighbourhood community mosque Accessible sermons Children's classes Daily community life
**Fun Fact:**Masjid Bilal was built by community fundraising in 1975 — each household in the original I-8 sector contributed to its construction, making it literally a collectively owned community institution.
10

## Blue Area Juma Mosque
Blue Area, Jinnah Avenue
The central mosque in Islamabad's commercial Blue Area serves the thousands of office workers, shopkeepers, and visitors who populate Pakistan's most important business district. The mosque fills completely at every Jumu'ah prayer as hundreds pour out of surrounding office towers to attend. The architecture is functional modernism — clean lines, quality marble, and excellent acoustics. The location at the heart of government and corporate Islamabad means Friday sermons here occasionally address national affairs and Islamic guidance on contemporary issues facing Pakistan's professional class.
Business district mosque High weekday attendance Clean modernist design Corporate congregation
**Fun Fact:**The Blue Area mosque experiences its highest attendance during Ramadan Tarawih prayers — the cooler nights during Ramadan in Islamabad make the outdoor overflow area pleasant, and attendance often exceeds 3,000 on peak nights.

## Final Thoughts
Islamabad's mosques form a spiritual geography that is inseparable from the city's identity. The Faisal Mosque stands at the northern end of the capital's ceremonial axis as the most recognisable building in Pakistan, while neighbourhood mosques like Masjid Bilal in I-8 represent the daily texture of Islamic community life across the sectors. Between these poles lies a remarkable range of architectural approaches to the same spiritual purpose. For visitors, the single most rewarding mosque experience is arriving at the Faisal Mosque at dawn for Fajr prayer — the light on the white marble, the echo of the call across the courtyard, and the Margalla Hills emerging from darkness behind the minarets is an experience of extraordinary beauty and spiritual power. Equally moving is attending Friday Jumu'ah at Lal Masjid, where the weight of history and decades of community memory fill every corner of the red sandstone space.
10

After 36 years, Islamabad’s iconic Faisal Mosque is set to undergo major renovation with support from Saudi Arabia. Built in 1988 and designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, the mosque stands as a symbol of the capital.
The Capital Development Authority (CDA) is preparing a memorandum of understanding with the Saudi government to formalize assistance.
During a recent meeting, CDA Chairman Mohammad Ali Randhawa and Saudi Ambassador Nawaf bin Said Al-Malki also discussed investments in Islamabad’s hotel sector and preparations for Saudi National Day.

**Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences** (انسٹی ٹیوٹ علوم طبی پاکستان) is a research oriented health sciences institute located in Islamabad, Pakistan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-TNI-2)
It is one of the region's leading tertiary level hospitals which includes 22 medical and surgical specialist centers. It provides medical training through the _Quaid-e-Azam Postgraduate Medical College_ which was established on 1 February 1989.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-3)
Later on Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University was established through act of parliament in 2013. The first vice chancellor was professor Dr. Javed Akram who served till 2018.

Established in 1985 the institute includes three semi-autonomous hospitals including the Islamabad Hospital (IH) which is a 592-bed hospital spread over 3.5 hectares, the 230 bedded Children's Hospital spread over 1.6 hectares specializing in pediatric care and the 125 bedded Maternal & Child Health Care Centre which specializes in obstetrics and gynecology.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-PIMS-5)
On 26 August 2026, a fire broke out at the hospital's maternity ward, killing 14 infants.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-6)
On 26 August 2026, a fire broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit of the Mother and Child Health ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad, Pakistan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-7) Fourteen newborns died in the incident, while one infant was rescued. An inquiry was subsequently launched into the cause of the fire and the hospital's fire-safety and emergency procedures.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-8)

Title: Shifa International Hospitals Ltd. | Devex
Chunks: 0,1
The Hospital was incorporated on**September 20, 1987**as a Private Limited Company and converted into Public Limited Company on October 12, 1989. The first Shifa office was established at the residence of Dr. Zaheer Ahmad in sector F-8/3 of Islamabad. Later it was moved to a rental place in Blue Area (commercial buildings area in Islamabad), and finally the site office building was established in January 1988.
The construction activity to prepare the site for laying the foundation of the Hospital was started in the beginning of 1988. The foundation ceremony took place on**October 06, 1989**by the parents and well-wishers of the sponsors and their dedicated team of colleagues and well- wishers.
The idea of developing a high class medical facility in Pakistan was conceived in New York, USA in the mid of 1985. The initiator Dr. Zaheer Ahmad, who had just finished his Internal Medicine Residency, called a meeting at his apartment in Brooklyn, New York on the weekend of July 20 & 21. Five professionals gathered there and discussed the idea in detail and approved it. The participants included Dr. Manzoor H. Qazi from Leesville, Louisiana, Mr. Muhammad Zahid from Kew Gardens, New York, Mr. Samiullah Sharief from Brooklyn, New York, Dr. Sabir Ali from Palm Bay, Florida and Dr. Zaheer himself Dr. Zaheer Ahmad was asked to prepare the feasibility report and the action plan. Subsequently Dr. Zaheer Ahmad moved to Islamabad on December 17, 1985 to start the work on this project.
After extensive discussions and many meetings, the present site in the capital city of Islamabad was selected for this project. The name**SHIFA**was approved because of its comprehensiveness, originating from their culture, belief and values in totality.
After acquiring over 11 acres of land in Islamabad in 1987, CRI, a hospital development company in Princeton, New Jersey was hired to develop the plan and design of the project. Mr. William Parker, Chief Architect of CRI headed the team, visited the site in Islamabad besides visiting the other hospitals across Pakistan. CRI finished its job in 1989.

Shifa International Hospital offers 398 IPD beds with quality care and OPD facility in different specializations. Nevertheless it is an unending journey. People at Shifa are continuously striving hard to bring improvement and novelty with every passing moment.
Now after two decades, Shifa International Hospital proudly stands as a symbol of quality healthcare with its own brand name **SHIFA**. The short history of Shifa witnessed rare dedication and devotion of its consultants, management and staff who worked round the clock to make Shifa a reality of its own.
It was the vision of the founding Sponsors which took its shape into reality. The task was made possible only with the help of dedicated team of experts and managers under the quality-oriented and inspiring leadership.
Today, the hospital’s Block-A, B, C, D, E and F, ICU beds, new ORs etc., sprawled on its site are efficiently functioning. Allah’s grace made it feasible and viable to carry out such a gigantic and enormous venture. Unique in its concept and efforts set up by the expatriate Pakistanis to repay their homeland with a beautiful gift in the form of a functional institution in the healthcare industry of Pakistan.

**Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences** (انسٹی ٹیوٹ علوم طبی پاکستان) is a research oriented health sciences institute located in Islamabad, Pakistan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-TNI-2)
It is one of the region's leading tertiary level hospitals which includes 22 medical and surgical specialist centers. It provides medical training through the _Quaid-e-Azam Postgraduate Medical College_ which was established on 1 February 1989.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-3)
Later on Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University was established through act of parliament in 2013. The first vice chancellor was professor Dr. Javed Akram who served till 2018.
texts.1:
Established in 1985 the institute includes three semi-autonomous hospitals including the Islamabad Hospital (IH) which is a 592-bed hospital spread over 3.5 hectares, the 230 bedded Children's Hospital spread over 1.6 hectares specializing in pediatric care and the 125 bedded Maternal & Child Health Care Centre which specializes in obstetrics and gynecology.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-PIMS-5)
On 26 August 2026, a fire broke out at the hospital's maternity ward, killing 14 infants.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-6)
On 26 August 2026, a fire broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit of the Mother and Child Health ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad, Pakistan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-7) Fourteen newborns died in the incident, while one infant was rescued. An inquiry was subsequently launched into the cause of the fire and the hospital's fire-safety and emergency procedures.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-8)

After 36 years, Islamabad’s iconic Faisal Mosque is set to undergo major renovation with support from Saudi Arabia. Built in 1988 and designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, the mosque stands as a symbol of the capital.
The Capital Development Authority (CDA) is preparing a memorandum of understanding with the Saudi government to formalize assistance.
During a recent meeting, CDA Chairman Mohammad Ali Randhawa and Saudi Ambassador Nawaf bin Said Al-Malki also discussed investments in Islamabad’s hotel sector and preparations for Saudi National Day.
The renovation aims to preserve the mosque’s architectural legacy while strengthening Pakistan-Saudi cultural ties.

## PAK - CHINA FRIENDSHIP HOSPITAL ISLAMABAD
Pak-China Friendship Hospital Islamabad is a **160-bed** secondary care hospital on Kuri Road, Islamabad, run by The Indus Hospital & Health Network (IHHN) through a public-private partnership with the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination. The facility has grown from a single-purpose infection control facility into a full-service hospital serving approximately **200,000** patients per year.

**Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences** (انسٹی ٹیوٹ علوم طبی پاکستان) is a research oriented health sciences institute located in Islamabad, Pakistan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-TNI-2)
It is one of the region's leading tertiary level hospitals which includes 22 medical and surgical specialist centers. It provides medical training through the _Quaid-e-Azam Postgraduate Medical College_ which was established on 1 February 1989.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-3)
Later on Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University was established through act of parliament in 2013. The first vice chancellor was professor Dr. Javed Akram who served till 2018.

Established in 1985 the institute includes three semi-autonomous hospitals including the Islamabad Hospital (IH) which is a 592-bed hospital spread over 3.5 hectares, the 230 bedded Children's Hospital spread over 1.6 hectares specializing in pediatric care and the 125 bedded Maternal & Child Health Care Centre which specializes in obstetrics and gynecology.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-PIMS-5)
On 26 August 2026, a fire broke out at the hospital's maternity ward, killing 14 infants.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-6)
On 26 August 2026, a fire broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit of the Mother and Child Health ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad, Pakistan.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Institute_of_Medical_Sciences#cite_note-7) Fourteen newborns died in the incident, while one infant was rescued. The Hospital was incorporated on**September 20, 1987**as a Private Limited Company and converted into Public Limited Company on October 12, 1989. The first Shifa office was established at the residence of Dr. Zaheer Ahmad in sector F-8/3 of Islamabad. Later it was moved to a rental place in Blue Area (commercial buildings area in Islamabad), and finally the site office building was established in January 1988.
The construction activity to prepare the site for laying the foundation of the Hospital was started in the beginning of 1988. The foundation ceremony took place on**October 06, 1989**by the parents and well-wishers of the sponsors and their dedicated team of colleagues and well- wishers.
The idea of developing a high class medical facility in Pakistan was conceived in New York, USA in the mid of 1985. The initiator Dr. Zaheer Ahmad, who had just finished his Internal Medicine Residency, called a meeting at his apartment in Brooklyn, New York on the weekend of July 20 & 21. Five professionals gathered there and discussed the idea in detail and approved it. The participants included Dr. Manzoor H. Qazi from Leesville, Louisiana, Mr. Muhammad Zahid from Kew Gardens, New York, Mr. Samiullah Sharief from Brooklyn, New York, Dr. Sabir Ali from Palm Bay, Florida and Dr. Zaheer himself Dr. Zaheer Ahmad was asked to prepare the feasibility report and the action plan. Subsequently Dr. Zaheer Ahmad moved to Islamabad on December 17, 1985 to start the work on this project.
After extensive discussions and many meetings, the present site in the capital city of Islamabad was selected for this project. The name**SHIFA**was approved because of its comprehensiveness, originating from their culture, belief and values in totality.
After acquiring over 11 acres of land in Islamabad in 1987, CRI, a hospital development company in Princeton, New Jersey was hired to develop the plan and design of the project. Mr. William Parker, Chief Architect of CRI headed the team, visited the site in Islamabad besides visiting the other hospitals across Pakistan. CRI finished its job in 1989.

Shifa International Hospital offers 398 IPD beds with quality care and OPD facility in different specializations. Nevertheless it is an unending journey. People at Shifa are continuously striving hard to bring improvement and novelty with every passing moment.
Now after two decades, Shifa International Hospital proudly stands as a symbol of quality healthcare with its own brand name **SHIFA**. The short history of Shifa witnessed rare dedication and devotion of its consultants, management and staff who worked round the clock to make Shifa a reality of its own.
It was the vision of the founding Sponsors which took its shape into reality. The task was made possible only with the help of dedicated team of experts and managers under the quality-oriented and inspiring leadership.
Today, the hospital’s Block-A, B, C, D, E and F, ICU beds, new ORs etc., sprawled on its site are efficiently functioning. Allah’s grace made it feasible and viable to carry out such a gigantic and enormous venture. Unique in its concept and efforts set up by the expatriate Pakistanis to repay their homeland with a beautiful gift in the form of a functional institution in the healthcare industry of Pakistan.

The **Faisal Mosque**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-1) is the national mosque of Pakistan, located in Islamabad, the capital of the country.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-mosque1-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-mosque2-3) It is the sixth-largest mosque in the world and located on the foothills of Margalla Hills. It is named after the late King Faisal of Saudi Arabia (r.1964–75). Designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, the mosque features a contemporary design consisting of eight sides of concrete shell and is inspired by the design of a typical Bedouin tent.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Tribune-4)

A major tourist attraction in Pakistan, the mosque is a contemporary and influential piece of Islamic architecture. Famous spots including the mosque as a masterpiece of modern Islamic architecture, and the Pakistan Monument, which represents the country’s cultural history, add to the city’s charm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-TNI-5)
Construction of the mosque began in 1976 after a $28 million grant from Saudi King Faisal, whose name the mosque bears.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-timesnotgift-6) The unconventional design by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay was selected after an international competition.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-7) Without a typical dome, the mosque is shaped like a Bedouin tent, surrounded by four 90 m (300 ft)-tall minarets. The design features eight-sided shell shaped sloping roofs forming a triangular worship hall which can hold 10,000 worshippers.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-8)
Combined the structure covers an area of 130,000 square metres (33 acres), the mosque dominates the landscape of Islamabad.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-timesnotgift-6) It is situated at the north end of Faisal Avenue, putting it at the northernmost end of the city and at the foot of Margalla Hills, the westernmost foothills of the Himalayas. It is located on an elevated area of land against a picturesque backdrop of the national park. Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world from 1986 until 1993 when it was overtaken by the mosques in Saudi Arabia. It is now the sixth-largest mosque in the world in terms of capacity.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Tribune3-10)
Aerial view

The impetus for the mosque began in 1966 when King Faisal bin Abdul-Aziz supported the initiative of the Pakistani Government to build a national mosque in Islamabad during an official visit to Pakistan. In 1969, an international competition was held in which architects from 17 countries submitted 43 proposals. The winning design was that of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay. 190,000 m 2; 2,000,000 ft 2 of land were assigned for the project and the execution was assigned to Pakistani engineers and workers.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-11) Construction of the mosque began in 1976 by National Construction Limited of Pakistan, led by Azim Khan and was funded by the government of Saudi Arabia, at a cost of over 130 million Saudi riyals (approximately 120 million USD today). King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz was instrumental in the funding, and both the mosque and the road leading to it were named after him after his assassination in 1975. King Faisal bin Abdulaziz's successor King Khalid laid the foundation stone for the mosque in October 1976[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-12) and signed the construction agreement in 1978. Basic information about the mosque can be found written on the foundation stone. On 18 June 1988, the first prayer was held, although the mosque was completed in 1986. The mosque grounds along with being a building for prayer also used to house the International Islamic University some years ago but has since relocated to a new campus in 2000. Some traditional and conservative Muslims criticised the design at first for its unconventional design and lack of a traditional dome structure.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-13)
Interior view

The mosque can accommodate about 300,000 worshippers. Each of the Mosque's four minarets are 90 metres (300 ft) high (the tallest minarets in South Asia) and measure 10×10 metres in circumference.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-13) The main areas have the capacity to hold up to 74000 people in the main areas including the inner hall, and the courtyards. The grounds around the mosque have the capacity to contain up to 200,000 people.
> I tried to capture the spirit, proportion, and geometry of Kaaba in a purely abstract manner. Imagine the apex of each of the four minarets as a scaled explosion of four highest corners of Kaaba – thus an unseen Kaaba form is bounded by the minarets at the four corners in a proportion of height to base. Shah Faisal Mosque is akin to the Holy Kaaba in the designer's imaginative eyes. Now, if you join the apex of each minaret to the base of the minaret diagonally opposite to it correspondingly, a four-sided pyramid shall be bound by these lines at the base side within that invisible cube. That lower level pyramid is treated as a solid body while four minarets with their apex complete the imaginary cube of Kaaba.
—Vedat Dalokay, "Dalokay further explaining the thinking behind the design of the Masjid to students of a design school."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Embassy-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-PakistanToday-15)
Faisal Mosque close-up view during night

Title: Faisal Mosque!
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
The **Faisal Mosque** (Urdu: فیصل مسجد‎) is the largest mosque in Pakistan, located in the national capital city ofIslamabad. Completed in 1986, it was designed by TurkisharchitectVedat Dalokay, shaped like a desert Bedouin’s tent, is an iconic symbol of Islamabad throughout the world.
It is situated at the north end of Faisal Avenue, putting it at the northernmost end of the city and at the foot ofMargalla Hills, the westernmost foothills of the Himalayas. It is located on an elevated area of land against a picturesque backdrop of the Margalla Hills. This enviable location represents the mosque’s great importance and allows it to be seen from miles around day and night.
The Faisal Mosque was conceived as the National Mosque of Pakistan and named after the late KingFaisal bin Abdul-Aziz of Saudi Arabia, who supported and financed the project.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Mass-2)
The largest mosque in South Asia, the Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world from 1986 until 1993, when it was overtaken in size by the newly completed Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca, Morocco. Subsequent expansions of the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque) of Mecca and the Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (Prophet’s Mosque) inMedina, Saudi Arabia, during the 1990s relegated Faisal Mosque to fourth place in terms of size.

Coordinates: 33.729944°N 73.038436°ECoordinates: 33.729944°N 73.038436°E  
LocationIslamabad, Pakistan  
Established 1987  
Architectural information  
Architect(s)Vedat Dalokay  
StyleContemporary Islamic  
Capacity 74,000 within the main areas,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) approx. 200,000 in adjoining grounds  
Covered area 5,000 m 2 (54,000 sq ft)  
Minaret(s)4  
Minaret height 90 m (300 ft)  
Construction cost 120 million USD

## History
The impetus for the mosque began in 1966 when King Faisal bin Abdul-Azizsupported the initiative of the Pakistani Government to build a national mosque in Islamabad during an official visit to Pakistan.
In 1969, an international competition was held in which architects from 17 countries submitted 43 proposals. The winning design was that of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Rengel-3) Construction of the mosque began in 1976 by National Construction of Pakistan, led by Azim Khan and was funded by the government of Saudi Arabia, at a cost of over 130 million Saudi riyals (approximately 120 million USD today). King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz was instrumental in the funding, and both the mosque and the road leading to it were named after him after his assassination in 1975. The mosque was completed in 1986, and used to house the International Islamic University. Many conservative Muslims criticised the design at first for its unconventional design and lack of a traditional dome structure, but most criticism ended when the completed mosque’s scale, form, and setting against the Margalla Hills became evident.

## Design
The Faisal Mosque is the work of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, who won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the project. The mosque’s architecture is modern and unique, lacking both the traditional domes and arches of most other mosques around the world.
Shah Faisal Masjid, also known as Faisal Mosque, located in the start of Margala hill sector E-7 Islamabad Pakistan
The mosque’s unusual design is a departure from the long history of South Asian Islamic architecture, fusing contemporary lines with the more traditional look of an ArabBedouin‘s tent, with its large triangular prayer hall and four minarets. However, unlike traditional masjid design, it lacks a dome. The minarets borrow their design from Turkish tradition and are thin and pencil like.
Interior of Faisal Mosque
The shape of the Faisal Mosque is an eight-sided concrete shell inspired by a desert Beduoin’s tent and the cubic Kaabain Mecca, flanked by four unusual minarets inspired by Turkish architecture. The architect later explained his thinking to design school students:[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-4)
“I tried to capture the spirit, proportion and geometry of Kaaba in a purely abstract manner. Imagine the apex of each of the four minaret as a scaled explosion of four highest corners of Kaaba – thus an unseen Kaaba form is bounded by the minarets at the four corners in a proportion of height to base. Shah Faisal Mosque akin to Kaaba.
Now, if you join the apex of each minaret to the base of the minaret diagonally opposite to it correspondingly, a four-sided pyramid shall be bound by these lines at the base side within that invisible cube. That lower level pyramid is treated as a solid body while four minarets with their apex complete the imaginary cube of Kaaba.”

## Design
Entrance is from the east, where the prayer hall is fronted by a courtyard with porticoes. The International Islamic University was housed under the main courtyard, but recently relocated to a new campus. The mosque still houses a library, lecture hall, museum and cafe. The interior of the main tent-shaped hall is covered in white marble and decorated with mosaics and calligraphy by the famous Pakistani artist Sadequain, and a spectacular Turkish-style chandelier. The mosaic pattern adorns the west wall, and has the _kalimah_ written in early Kuficscript, repeated in mirror image pattern. Nekka Phullai is the adjacent hill to the mosque in Margalla Hills.

## Capacity
Interior of the mosque.
The Faisal Mosque has covered area of 5,000 m 2 (54,000 sq ft). It can accommodate 10,000 worshipers in its main prayer hall,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) 24,000 in its porticoes,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) 40,000 in its courtyard,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) and another 200,000 in its adjoining grounds_[citation needed_]. Although its covered main prayer hall is smaller than that of the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca (the world’s third largest mosque), Faisal Mosque has the third largest capacity of accommodating worshipers in its adjoining grounds after the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque) of Mecca, the Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (Prophet’s Mosque) in Medina_[citation needed_]. Each of the Mosque’s four minarets are 80 m (260 ft) high (the tallest minarets in South Asia) and measure 10 x 10 m in circumference.

## References in literature
The Faisal Mosque is described in the book _The Kite Runner_ by Khalid Hosseini, and is frequently referenced in the work of Michael Muhammad Knight, who came to the mosque to study Islam as a teenager.

The **Faisal Mosque**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-1) is the national mosque of Pakistan, located in Islamabad, the capital of the country.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-mosque1-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-mosque2-3) It is the sixth-largest mosque in the world and located on the foothills of Margalla Hills. It is named after the late King Faisal of Saudi Arabia (r.1964–75). Designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, the mosque features a contemporary design consisting of eight sides of concrete shell and is inspired by the design of a typical Bedouin tent.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Tribune-4)
texts.1:
A major tourist attraction in Pakistan, the mosque is a contemporary and influential piece of Islamic architecture. Famous spots including the mosque as a masterpiece of modern Islamic architecture, and the Pakistan Monument, which represents the country’s cultural history, add to the city’s charm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-TNI-5)
Construction of the mosque began in 1976 after a $28 million grant from Saudi King Faisal, whose name the mosque bears.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-timesnotgift-6) The unconventional design by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay was selected after an international competition.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-7) Without a typical dome, the mosque is shaped like a Bedouin tent, surrounded by four 90 m (300 ft)-tall minarets. The design features eight-sided shell shaped sloping roofs forming a triangular worship hall which can hold 10,000 worshippers.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-8)
Combined the structure covers an area of 130,000 square metres (33 acres), the mosque dominates the landscape of Islamabad.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-timesnotgift-6) It is situated at the north end of Faisal Avenue, putting it at the northernmost end of the city and at the foot of Margalla Hills, the westernmost foothills of the Himalayas. It is located on an elevated area of land against a picturesque backdrop of the national park. Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world from 1986 until 1993 when it was overtaken by the mosques in Saudi Arabia. It is now the sixth-largest mosque in the world in terms of capacity.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Tribune3-10)
Aerial view
texts.2:
The impetus for the mosque began in 1966 when King Faisal bin Abdul-Aziz supported the initiative of the Pakistani Government to build a national mosque in Islamabad during an official visit to Pakistan. In 1969, an international competition was held in which architects from 17 countries submitted 43 proposals. The winning design was that of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay. 190,000 m 2; 2,000,000 ft 2 of land were assigned for the project and the execution was assigned to Pakistani engineers and workers.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-11) Construction of the mosque began in 1976 by National Construction Limited of Pakistan, led by Azim Khan and was funded by the government of Saudi Arabia, at a cost of over 130 million Saudi riyals (approximately 120 million USD today). King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz was instrumental in the funding, and both the mosque and the road leading to it were named after him after his assassination in 1975. King Faisal bin Abdulaziz's successor King Khalid laid the foundation stone for the mosque in October 1976[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-12) and signed the construction agreement in 1978. Basic information about the mosque can be found written on the foundation stone. On 18 June 1988, the first prayer was held, although the mosque was completed in 1986. The mosque grounds along with being a building for prayer also used to house the International Islamic University some years ago but has since relocated to a new campus in 2000. Some traditional and conservative Muslims criticised the design at first for its unconventional design and lack of a traditional dome structure.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-13)
Interior view
texts.3:
The mosque can accommodate about 300,000 worshippers. Each of the Mosque's four minarets are 90 metres (300 ft) high (the tallest minarets in South Asia) and measure 10×10 metres in circumference.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-13) The main areas have the capacity to hold up to 74000 people in the main areas including the inner hall, and the courtyards. The grounds around the mosque have the capacity to contain up to 200,000 people.
> I tried to capture the spirit, proportion, and geometry of Kaaba in a purely abstract manner. Imagine the apex of each of the four minarets as a scaled explosion of four highest corners of Kaaba – thus an unseen Kaaba form is bounded by the minarets at the four corners in a proportion of height to base. Shah Faisal Mosque is akin to the Holy Kaaba in the designer's imaginative eyes. Now, if you join the apex of each minaret to the base of the minaret diagonally opposite to it correspondingly, a four-sided pyramid shall be bound by these lines at the base side within that invisible cube. That lower level pyramid is treated as a solid body while four minarets with their apex complete the imaginary cube of Kaaba.
—Vedat Dalokay, "Dalokay further explaining the thinking behind the design of the Masjid to students of a design school."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Embassy-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-PakistanToday-15)
Faisal Mosque close-up view during night

The **Faisal Mosque** (Urdu: فیصل مسجد‎) is the largest mosque in Pakistan, located in the national capital city ofIslamabad. Completed in 1986, it was designed by TurkisharchitectVedat Dalokay, shaped like a desert Bedouin’s tent, is an iconic symbol of Islamabad throughout the world.
It is situated at the north end of Faisal Avenue, putting it at the northernmost end of the city and at the foot ofMargalla Hills, the westernmost foothills of the Himalayas. It is located on an elevated area of land against a picturesque backdrop of the Margalla Hills. This enviable location represents the mosque’s great importance and allows it to be seen from miles around day and night.
The Faisal Mosque was conceived as the National Mosque of Pakistan and named after the late KingFaisal bin Abdul-Aziz of Saudi Arabia, who supported and financed the project.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Mass-2)
The largest mosque in South Asia, the Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world from 1986 until 1993, when it was overtaken in size by the newly completed Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca, Morocco. Subsequent expansions of the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque) of Mecca and the Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (Prophet’s Mosque) inMedina, Saudi Arabia, during the 1990s relegated Faisal Mosque to fourth place in terms of size.

texts.2:
## History
The impetus for the mosque began in 1966 when King Faisal bin Abdul-Azizsupported the initiative of the Pakistani Government to build a national mosque in Islamabad during an official visit to Pakistan.
In 1969, an international competition was held in which architects from 17 countries submitted 43 proposals. The winning design was that of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Rengel-3) Construction of the mosque began in 1976 by National Construction of Pakistan, led by Azim Khan and was funded by the government of Saudi Arabia, at a cost of over 130 million Saudi riyals (approximately 120 million USD today). King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz was instrumental in the funding, and both the mosque and the road leading to it were named after him after his assassination in 1975. The mosque was completed in 1986, and used to house the International Islamic University. Many conservative Muslims criticised the design at first for its unconventional design and lack of a traditional dome structure, but most criticism ended when the completed mosque’s scale, form, and setting against the Margalla Hills became evident.
texts.3:
## Design
The Faisal Mosque is the work of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, who won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the project. The mosque’s architecture is modern and unique, lacking both the traditional domes and arches of most other mosques around the world.
Shah Faisal Masjid, also known as Faisal Mosque, located in the start of Margala hill sector E-7 Islamabad Pakistan
The mosque’s unusual design is a departure from the long history of South Asian Islamic architecture, fusing contemporary lines with the more traditional look of an ArabBedouin‘s tent, with its large triangular prayer hall and four minarets. However, unlike traditional masjid design, it lacks a dome. The minarets borrow their design from Turkish tradition and are thin and pencil like.
Interior of Faisal Mosque
The shape of the Faisal Mosque is an eight-sided concrete shell inspired by a desert Beduoin’s tent and the cubic Kaabain Mecca, flanked by four unusual minarets inspired by Turkish architecture. The architect later explained his thinking to design school students:[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-4)
“I tried to capture the spirit, proportion and geometry of Kaaba in a purely abstract manner. Imagine the apex of each of the four minaret as a scaled explosion of four highest corners of Kaaba – thus an unseen Kaaba form is bounded by the minarets at the four corners in a proportion of height to base. Shah Faisal Mosque akin to Kaaba.
Now, if you join the apex of each minaret to the base of the minaret diagonally opposite to it correspondingly, a four-sided pyramid shall be bound by these lines at the base side within that invisible cube. That lower level pyramid is treated as a solid body while four minarets with their apex complete the imaginary cube of Kaaba.”
texts.4:
## Design
Entrance is from the east, where the prayer hall is fronted by a courtyard with porticoes. The International Islamic University was housed under the main courtyard, but recently relocated to a new campus. The mosque still houses a library, lecture hall, museum and cafe. The interior of the main tent-shaped hall is covered in white marble and decorated with mosaics and calligraphy by the famous Pakistani artist Sadequain, and a spectacular Turkish-style chandelier. The mosaic pattern adorns the west wall, and has the _kalimah_ written in early Kuficscript, repeated in mirror image pattern. Nekka Phullai is the adjacent hill to the mosque in Margalla Hills.
texts.5:
## Capacity
Interior of the mosque.
The Faisal Mosque has covered area of 5,000 m 2 (54,000 sq ft). It can accommodate 10,000 worshipers in its main prayer hall,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) 24,000 in its porticoes,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) 40,000 in its courtyard,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) and another 200,000 in its adjoining grounds_[citation needed_]. Although its covered main prayer hall is smaller than that of the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca (the world’s third largest mosque), Faisal Mosque has the third largest capacity of accommodating worshipers in its adjoining grounds after the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque) of Mecca, the Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (Prophet’s Mosque) in Medina_[citation needed_]. Each of the Mosque’s four minarets are 80 m (260 ft) high (the tallest minarets in South Asia) and measure 10 x 10 m in circumference.
texts.6:
## References in literature
The Faisal Mosque is described in the book _The Kite Runner_ by Khalid Hosseini, and is frequently referenced in the work of Michael Muhammad Knight, who came to the mosque to study Islam as a teenager.

The **Faisal Mosque**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-1) is the national mosque of Pakistan, located in Islamabad, the capital of the country.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-mosque1-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-mosque2-3) It is the sixth-largest mosque in the world and located on the foothills of Margalla Hills. It is named after the late King Faisal of Saudi Arabia (r.1964–75). Designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, the mosque features a contemporary design consisting of eight sides of concrete shell and is inspired by the design of a typical Bedouin tent.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Tribune-4)

A major tourist attraction in Pakistan, the mosque is a contemporary and influential piece of Islamic architecture. Famous spots including the mosque as a masterpiece of modern Islamic architecture, and the Pakistan Monument, which represents the country’s cultural history, add to the city’s charm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-TNI-5)
Construction of the mosque began in 1976 after a $28 million grant from Saudi King Faisal, whose name the mosque bears.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-timesnotgift-6) The unconventional design by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay was selected after an international competition.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-7) Without a typical dome, the mosque is shaped like a Bedouin tent, surrounded by four 90 m (300 ft)-tall minarets. The design features eight-sided shell shaped sloping roofs forming a triangular worship hall which can hold 10,000 worshippers.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-8)
Combined the structure covers an area of 130,000 square metres (33 acres), the mosque dominates the landscape of Islamabad.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-timesnotgift-6) It is situated at the north end of Faisal Avenue, putting it at the northernmost end of the city and at the foot of Margalla Hills, the westernmost foothills of the Himalayas. It is located on an elevated area of land against a picturesque backdrop of the national park. Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world from 1986 until 1993 when it was overtaken by the mosques in Saudi Arabia. It is now the sixth-largest mosque in the world in terms of capacity.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Tribune3-10)
Aerial view

The impetus for the mosque began in 1966 when King Faisal bin Abdul-Aziz supported the initiative of the Pakistani Government to build a national mosque in Islamabad during an official visit to Pakistan. In 1969, an international competition was held in which architects from 17 countries submitted 43 proposals. The winning design was that of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay. 190,000 m 2; 2,000,000 ft 2 of land were assigned for the project and the execution was assigned to Pakistani engineers and workers.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-11) Construction of the mosque began in 1976 by National Construction Limited of Pakistan, led by Azim Khan and was funded by the government of Saudi Arabia, at a cost of over 130 million Saudi riyals (approximately 120 million USD today). King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz was instrumental in the funding, and both the mosque and the road leading to it were named after him after his assassination in 1975. King Faisal bin Abdulaziz's successor King Khalid laid the foundation stone for the mosque in October 1976[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-12) and signed the construction agreement in 1978. Basic information about the mosque can be found written on the foundation stone. On 18 June 1988, the first prayer was held, although the mosque was completed in 1986. The mosque grounds along with being a building for prayer also used to house the International Islamic University some years ago but has since relocated to a new campus in 2000. Some traditional and conservative Muslims criticised the design at first for its unconventional design and lack of a traditional dome structure.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-13)
Interior view

The mosque can accommodate about 300,000 worshippers. The **Faisal Mosque** (Urdu: فیصل مسجد‎) is the largest mosque in Pakistan, located in the national capital city ofIslamabad. Completed in 1986, it was designed by TurkisharchitectVedat Dalokay, shaped like a desert Bedouin’s tent, is an iconic symbol of Islamabad throughout the world.
It is situated at the north end of Faisal Avenue, putting it at the northernmost end of the city and at the foot ofMargalla Hills, the westernmost foothills of the Himalayas. It is located on an elevated area of land against a picturesque backdrop of the Margalla Hills. This enviable location represents the mosque’s great importance and allows it to be seen from miles around day and night.
The Faisal Mosque was conceived as the National Mosque of Pakistan and named after the late KingFaisal bin Abdul-Aziz of Saudi Arabia, who supported and financed the project.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Mass-2)
The largest mosque in South Asia, the Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world from 1986 until 1993, when it was overtaken in size by the newly completed Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca, Morocco. Subsequent expansions of the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque) of Mecca and the Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (Prophet’s Mosque) inMedina, Saudi Arabia, during the 1990s relegated Faisal Mosque to fourth place in terms of size.

## History
The impetus for the mosque began in 1966 when King Faisal bin Abdul-Azizsupported the initiative of the Pakistani Government to build a national mosque in Islamabad during an official visit to Pakistan.
In 1969, an international competition was held in which architects from 17 countries submitted 43 proposals. The winning design was that of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-Rengel-3) Construction of the mosque began in 1976 by National Construction of Pakistan, led by Azim Khan and was funded by the government of Saudi Arabia, at a cost of over 130 million Saudi riyals (approximately 120 million USD today). King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz was instrumental in the funding, and both the mosque and the road leading to it were named after him after his assassination in 1975. The mosque was completed in 1986, and used to house the International Islamic University. Many conservative Muslims criticised the design at first for its unconventional design and lack of a traditional dome structure, but most criticism ended when the completed mosque’s scale, form, and setting against the Margalla Hills became evident.

## Design
The Faisal Mosque is the work of Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, who won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the project. The mosque’s architecture is modern and unique, lacking both the traditional domes and arches of most other mosques around the world.
Shah Faisal Masjid, also known as Faisal Mosque, located in the start of Margala hill sector E-7 Islamabad Pakistan
The mosque’s unusual design is a departure from the long history of South Asian Islamic architecture, fusing contemporary lines with the more traditional look of an ArabBedouin‘s tent, with its large triangular prayer hall and four minarets. However, unlike traditional masjid design, it lacks a dome. The minarets borrow their design from Turkish tradition and are thin and pencil like.
Interior of Faisal Mosque
The shape of the Faisal Mosque is an eight-sided concrete shell inspired by a desert Beduoin’s tent and the cubic Kaabain Mecca, flanked by four unusual minarets inspired by Turkish architecture. The architect later explained his thinking to design school students:[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-4)
“I tried to capture the spirit, proportion and geometry of Kaaba in a purely abstract manner. Imagine the apex of each of the four minaret as a scaled explosion of four highest corners of Kaaba – thus an unseen Kaaba form is bounded by the minarets at the four corners in a proportion of height to base. Shah Faisal Mosque akin to Kaaba.
Now, if you join the apex of each minaret to the base of the minaret diagonally opposite to it correspondingly, a four-sided pyramid shall be bound by these lines at the base side within that invisible cube. That lower level pyramid is treated as a solid body while four minarets with their apex complete the imaginary cube of Kaaba.”

## Design
Entrance is from the east, where the prayer hall is fronted by a courtyard with porticoes. The International Islamic University was housed under the main courtyard, but recently relocated to a new campus. The mosque still houses a library, lecture hall, museum and cafe. The interior of the main tent-shaped hall is covered in white marble and decorated with mosaics and calligraphy by the famous Pakistani artist Sadequain, and a spectacular Turkish-style chandelier. The mosaic pattern adorns the west wall, and has the _kalimah_ written in early Kuficscript, repeated in mirror image pattern. Nekka Phullai is the adjacent hill to the mosque in Margalla Hills.

## Capacity
Interior of the mosque.
The Faisal Mosque has covered area of 5,000 m 2 (54,000 sq ft). It can accommodate 10,000 worshipers in its main prayer hall,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) 24,000 in its porticoes,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) 40,000 in its courtyard,[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Mosque#cite_note-archnet-1) and another 200,000 in its adjoining grounds_[citation needed_]. Although its covered main prayer hall is smaller than that of the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca (the world’s third largest mosque), Faisal Mosque has the third largest capacity of accommodating worshipers in its adjoining grounds after the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque) of Mecca, the Al-Masjid al-Nabawi (Prophet’s Mosque) in Medina_[citation needed_]. Each of the Mosque’s four minarets are 80 m (260 ft) high (the tallest minarets in South Asia) and measure 10 x 10 m in circumference.

## References in literature
The Faisal Mosque is described in the book _The Kite Runner_ by Khalid Hosseini, and is frequently referenced in the work of Michael Muhammad Knight, who came to the mosque to study Islam as a teenager.
